articleTitle: An overview of transmission fault current limiters
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Fault Current Limiters - A Look at Tomorrow
abstract: Many designs of fault current limiter for use at power system voltages of 275 kV and greater have been proposed but it has not been clear which, if any, would be the most feasible and/or cost effective solution to the potential problem of increasing power system fault levels. This paper attempts to give an overview of the present situation and indicate the designs most likely to succeed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Fault Current Limiters - A Look at Tomorrow
abstract: Three different superconducting fault limiter designs are described in relation to low temperature (metallic) superconductors operating at 4.2 K and high temperature (ceramic) superconductor at 77 K. The three devices described are: a resistive superconducting fault current limiter (SCFCL); a saturated inductive SCFCL; and a shielded inductive SCFCL. Resistive type SCFCLs operating at 4.2 K are being considered for application by some utilities, despite being harnessed with the technology and operating costs associated with using liquid helium; the relatively low weight and volume makes it attractive in some applications. The shielded inductive type incorporating high T/sub c/ superconductor discs may be considered the most practical. Using near term state-of-the-art technology and operating at 77 K with bulk liquid nitrogen would make the device virtually maintenance free and life time expectancy should be in excess of 30-40 years.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A static fault current limiting and interrupting device
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Fault Current Limiters - A Look at Tomorrow
abstract: A new fault current limiting and interrupting device (FCLID) is proposed and analyzed. The proposed FCLID can limit the fault current as well as being able to interrupt it. The proposed device has a simple structure, fast response, and is well suited to the duty required. In this device, the GTO thyristors contribute to the current limiting action, and the parallel impedance is replaced by a nonlinear resistor (varistor). The FCLID offers the following additional advantages. It can be designed to do a self-testing routine periodically, thus its reliable operation can always be checked and maintained. The FCLID can be designed to close or reclose each phase of the circuit (after complete fault interruption) at the suitable instant which produces minimum transients. In addition, the FCLID offers the ability to switch the power circuit ON and OFF via a remote control signal. Finally, the deployment of varistors across the GTO thyristors facilitate GTO series connection which is necessary for high voltage applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Superconducting fault current limiters based on high Tc superconductors
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Fault Current Limiters - A Look at Tomorrow
abstract: The worldwide increasing demand for electrical power leads to a growing interconnection of electrical networks. As a consequence, short-circuit currents (I/sub sc/) increase, leading to high mechanical and thermal stresses. All electrical equipment has to be designed to withstand these stresses. It is obvious, from both technical and economical points of view, that a device that reduces the I/sub sc/ is needed. All the solutions realized up to now have substantial disadvantages. They fulfil only a few of the characteristics expected of an ideal fault current limiter. The advantages and disadvantages of high temperature superconductors for fault current limiters are briefly mentioned. The authors then discuss the main concepts of superconducting fault limiters, the ABB concept of a shielded iron core, and the construction of a 100 kVA prototype and its testing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Thyristor control for fault current limitation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Fault Current Limiters - A Look at Tomorrow
abstract: Fast growing power networks with increasing fault levels may require the use of fault current limiting techniques. Thyristor-controlled schemes which insert a reactor or an inductive impedance can effectively reduce and limit fault currents. Several possibilities are well known, such as switched reactors and controlled series compensation. Other technologies, e.g. SMES and UPFC, are still under development or under study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High temperature superconductors for fault current limitation on local power distribution networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Fault Current Limiters - A Look at Tomorrow
abstract: The author describes the need for fault current limiters on local distribution networks. He considers the use of high temperature superconductors for such protection applications, and concludes with a brief consideration of some advanced materials processing techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
